headline: New Orleans buys its taste locally and its volume in the suburbs: Magazine Street and homegrown fleur-de-lis brands set the look, while Metairie malls, Dillard's and Dick's move the units.
summary: Basketball retail here is thin next to football and Mardi Gras. The Saints and local city-pride brands own the Gulf South gear wallet, and the Pelicans sit below them. Taste lives in a few uptown and Bywater shops plus pop-ups at second lines, festivals and Black-owned culture spaces. Volume lives in Metairie, Gretna and Kenner, and online. A Nike door strategy here is mostly about winning city-pride credibility, not adding square footage. After back-to-back sub-30-win seasons and a new coach in Jamahl Mosley, Zion and Trey Murphy III are the only real Pelicans retail pulls.

insights.title: The Saints wallet and city-pride brands outsell the Pelicans
insights.detail: Fleur-de-lis, 'Who Dat' and NOLA-pride tees from local brands like Dirty Coast and Fleurty Girl are what locals wear daily. Pelicans gear competes for the same shirt-drawer slot, and Pelicans fans often wear city-first rather than team-first.
insights.implication: Lead Pelicans and City Edition product with New Orleans iconography first and the team mark second, so it passes as city pride rather than team merch.

insights.title: Taste is set on Magazine Street and in the Bywater and Marigny, volume in Jefferson Parish
insights.detail: Uptown Magazine Street holds the independent boutiques and vintage; the Lakeside, Riverwalk and West Bank (Oakwood) malls hold the athletic chains and department stores where families buy sneakers and jerseys.
insights.implication: Seed limited drops and collabs in tastemaker doors and local pop-ups, then flow mainstream colorways to Foot Locker, Dick's and Dillard's in the suburbs.

insights.title: Real sneaker culture is community-run, not boutique-led
insights.detail: New Orleans has fewer destination sneaker boutiques than Atlanta or Houston. Sneaker and hoops culture runs through school and AAU hoops, park courts, resale meetups and Black-owned apparel brands, and much of it sells through social media and pop-ups.
insights.implication: Fund activations with local creators and pop-up hosts rather than a single flagship, and treat Instagram-driven local sellers as the retail scene.

insights.title: The arena team store is a game-night door, not a destination
insights.detail: The Pelicans Team Store at Smoothie King Center and the arena's pop-up kiosks capture event-night buyers, and the season-ticket base is modest after two losing seasons. Fanatics and the team's online store carry the rest of the team-gear volume.
insights.implication: Use the arena store for City Edition launch moments, Zion and Trey Murphy III player-tee drops, and Cup-night giveaways, and keep inventory depth online.

insights.title: Tourists distort the French Quarter and Canal Street picture
insights.detail: Canal Place, Riverwalk and the Quarter's souvenir shops see huge traffic, but it is visitor spend on Saints, Mardi Gras and generic NOLA gear, not local basketball demand.
insights.implication: Treat tourist districts as brand-visibility and Mardi Gras-season merchandising spots, not as read-throughs for local Pelicans demand.

insights.title: Mardi Gras Indian and second-line imagery is a licensing and respect line
insights.detail: Suits, feathers and beadwork belong to specific Black neighborhood tribes and the social aid and pleasure clubs, and the community is protective of how they are used. Commercial lifting without credit has drawn criticism.
insights.implication: Work only through paid collaboration with named artists and clubs, and keep product abstracted from ceremonial imagery.

places.name: Smoothie King Center
places.why: Home of the Pelicans and the Pelicans Team Store, the single most important team-branded door for game-night buyers.

places.name: Magazine Street
places.why: Six miles of independent boutiques, vintage and local-brand shops that set taste for the city's style-conscious shoppers.

places.name: Lakeside Shopping Center
places.why: The suburban mall where Jefferson Parish families buy sneakers and team gear at the chains and Dillard's.

places.name: Riverwalk Outlets
places.why: Riverfront outlet and tourist-heavy mall near the convention center and arena corridor.

places.name: Oakwood Center
places.why: The main West Bank mall, serving a large Black and working-class suburban base of sneaker buyers.

places.name: St. Claude Avenue corridor
places.why: Art-and-music-driven corridor where pop-ups, markets and local makers show up.

places.name: Frenchmen Art Market
places.why: Evening market of local makers and artists, a natural spot for small collab or artist pop-ups.

places.name: Dillard University
places.why: One of the city's HBCU anchors alongside Xavier, a source of young Black shoppers and homecoming-season demand.

people.name: Zion Williamson
people.why: The franchise's biggest jersey and sneaker draw, whose availability drives team-gear sales more than any other factor.

people.name: Trey Murphy III
people.why: Breakout scorer averaging 21.5 ppg and the most credible second face for team product.

people.name: Derik Queen
people.why: Young piece of the post-Zion core for second-year-player and youth product.

people.name: Jeremiah Fears
people.why: Young guard who gives a youth-facing storyline for sneakers and apparel.

people.name: Big Freedia
people.why: Queen of Bounce and the best-known face of New Orleans bounce, a high-credibility collaborator for pop-ups if approached and paid properly.

people.name: Dirty Coast
people.why: Long-running New Orleans pride brand with Magazine Street retail, an obvious partner for city-first graphics.

people.name: Fleurty Girl
people.why: Homegrown NOLA tee and gift brand with devoted local following and multiple local doors.

moments.name: Pelicans home opener and City Edition launch
moments.why: The first window when new uniforms and player tees can be sold at the arena and in local doors.

moments.name: NBA Cup West Group B nights
moments.why: Pelicans open Cup play at the Clippers on Oct 30, with home Cup nights as giveaway and merchandise moments.

moments.name: Holiday gifting
moments.why: Peak seasonal volume at malls and online for jerseys, hoodies and sneakers.

moments.name: Carnival season and Mardi Gras
moments.why: Peak tourist and local merch season and the city's biggest cultural moment; purple, green and gold dominate every shop.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival
moments.why: Huge pop-up and collab season with a local and visitor crowd, and a traditional venue for Black-owned makers.

moments.name: Essence Festival of Culture
moments.why: Major Black cultural and consumer event at the Superdome and Smoothie King Center area, a prime brand and retail activation window.

moments.name: Saints season
moments.why: Competes directly for fan spend and storefront space through the fall.

designCues.cue: Mardi Gras purple, green and gold used as accent rather than full palette
designCues.source: Carnival's official colors, ubiquitous across city merchandise
designCues.use: Use as trim and lining accents on Pelicans product to nod to the city without looking like novelty gear.

designCues.source: Mardi Gras color scheme and Pelicans' own gold
designCues.use: Pair with Pelicans navy for a city-first colorway.
Base for Association and Icon products where the city cue sits as accent.

designCues.cue: Fleur-de-lis in a restrained, non-Saints execution
designCues.source: City emblem in common local use
designCues.use: Use as a tonal embossed or tonal-print detail so it reads as city, not Saints.

designCues.source: French Quarter and Garden District architecture
designCues.use: Fine-line tonal repeat on warm-ups or lining.

designCues.source: Local corner stores, po-boy shops and second-line banners

designCues.cue: Brass band and second-line parade energy
designCues.source: Tremé and Seventh Ward social aid and pleasure club tradition
designCues.use: Tell the story through collaboration and credit, not sacred or ceremonial imagery.

productHooks: A neighborhood-name capsule (Seventh Ward, Tremé, Central City, West Bank) with local graphic artists, sold first through Magazine Street and St. Claude partners and pop-ups.
Zion and Trey Murphy III player tees and hoodies timed to the home opener and Cup nights at the arena store.
A Mardi Gras-season city-pride drop in tonal fleur-de-lis and Carnival accents, sold through local brands like Dirty Coast and Fleurty Girl.
A Jefferson Parish and West Bank school and AAU hoops-focused youth pack through Dick's and the mall chains.
Essence Festival weekend capsule with Black New Orleans designers and artists, paid and credited.
watchouts: Do not use Mardi Gras Indian suit, feather or beadwork imagery without paid collaboration with named tribe members or artists.
Fleur-de-lis and 'Who Dat' overlap with Saints and New Orleans Saints licensing; confirm any Saints-adjacent marks before use.
Do not treat tourist-district sales as local Pelicans demand.
Pelicans fandom is thinner after two sub-30-win seasons; avoid overstocking team-branded volume.

districts.name: Magazine Street (Uptown to Garden District)
districts.profile: Long corridor of independent boutiques, vintage, local brands and cafes.
districts.shopper: Style-conscious locals, Tulane students, young professionals and visitors.

districts.name: Bywater / Marigny / St. Claude Avenue
districts.profile: Arts-and-music-driven corridor with markets, galleries and pop-up-friendly spaces.

districts.name: Lakeside Shopping Center (Metairie)
districts.profile: Suburban enclosed mall anchored by Dillard's with athletic and sneaker chains.
districts.shopper: Jefferson Parish families, teens and mainstream sneaker buyers.

districts.name: Oakwood Center (Gretna)
districts.profile: West Bank mall with department store and chain anchors.
districts.shopper: West Bank families and working-class shoppers, with strong Black consumer base.

districts.name: Riverwalk Outlets and Canal Place
districts.profile: Riverfront outlet mall and upscale downtown mall near the convention center and Quarter.
districts.shopper: Tourists, convention visitors and some locals.

districts.name: Smoothie King Center and CBD
districts.profile: Arena district adjacent to the Superdome.
